default.q.pointvp_n4-t13-q1.explanation: The structure 「〜かどうか」embeds a yes-or-no question within a larger sentence, meaning “whether or not ...”. It takes the plain form (普通形), but with nouns (N) and na-adjectives (A-na) in the present affirmative, 「だ」must be omitted completely; 「な」or 「の」must not be added. Thus, 「サリナさんが本当にいい人かどうか、ともだちに聞きました」means: “I asked my friend whether Salina was really a good person.” To avoid this common trap, remember that nouns and na-adjectives before 「かどうか」remain in their base form, as in 「暇かどうか」and 「本当かどうか」, without any additional particle or linking ending. Another example is: 「その話が本当かどうか、確かめてみます。」(I will check whether that story is true).

default.q.pointvp_n4-t13-q1.why.2: ✗ (c) The ending「な」is used with a na-adjective when it modifies a noun; it is not used before「〜かどうか」.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t13-q1.why.3: ✗ (d) The particle 「の」connects two nouns; it is not used to link a noun with 「〜かどうか」.

default.q.pointvp_n4-t13-q4.explanation: The pattern「material noun + から作られます」indicates that a product is made from an ingredient that has been processed or chemically transformed, so its original form is no longer clearly visible. I have continued using it for about ten years now.” A contrasting example is: 「子どもの時から、毎日日記を書き続けています。」(I have continued writing in my diary every day since I was a child.) Learners often confuse this with 「〜てくる」(choice a), but 「〜てくる」usually expresses a gradual change or process leading toward the present, whereas 「〜続ける」emphasizes the persistent continuation of the action itself.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t18-q10.why.0: ✗ (a) The pattern 「〜てきている」 generally indicates a gradual, cumulative change from the past to the present; a compound verb is more natural when referring to using a specific object.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t18-q10.why.1: ✗ (b) The pattern 「〜ていく」 describes an action or trend continuing from the present into the future, so it does not fit a point ten years in the past.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t18-q10.why.2: ✗ (c) The pattern「〜終わる」means to finish or complete an action, which is the opposite of the context, where the speaker still owns and wears the watch.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t18-q10.why.3: ✓ (d) The compound verb 「V (ます-stem) + 続ける」combined with 「〜ています」expresses continuation, showing that the person has continued using the object for 10 years.

Together, they connect the events over time: 「社会人になって」(after starting working) leads to the physical change「太ってきた」(gradually gaining weight). default.q.pointvp_n4-t18-q11.why.1: ✗ (b) なって comes second, following the noun to form the event-time phrase 「社会人になって」.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t18-q11.why.2: ✓ (c) 太って occupies the third position, marked by the star, and links directly to the auxiliary verb きた that follows.

✅ Correct answer: (b) 話し
This is the connective form obtained by removing ます from the V-ます form, which is needed to combine with the auxiliary verb「おわる」and form a compound verb expressing completion.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t18-q2.explanation: At JLPT N4, the pattern「V-ます stem + 終わる (おわる)」expresses the complete or deliberate completion of an action. Here, the Group 1 verb「話す」becomes the continuative form「話し」and combines with「おわってから」to mean "after finishing speaking." The complete sentence「はっぴょうしている人が話しおわってから質問してください。」means: "Please ask questions after the person giving the presentation has finished speaking." Compare:「この本を読み終わったら、返してください。」(Please return this book after you finish reading it.) Suffixes describing stages of an action, such as「～終わる」and「～始める」, always follow the ます stem, so dictionary-form and negative-form choices can be eliminated.

default.q.pointvp_n4-t18-q2.why.2: ✗ (c) 「話す」 is the dictionary form and cannot be attached directly to 「おわる」 to form a compound verb.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t18-q2.why.3: ✗ (d) 「話さない」is the short negative form (nai-form), so it cannot be combined with 「おわる」according to the grammar rules.

default.q.pointvp_n4-t18-q3.explanation: The pattern 「Vます (without ます) + 続ける（つづける）」describes an action or state that continues for a period of time without stopping. The complete sentence means: “Because I kept standing and waiting in front of the ramen shop for more than an hour, I became ravenously hungry.” Another example is: 「朝から雨が降りつづけています。」(It has been raining continuously since this morning.) default.q.pointvp_n4-t18-q3.why.0: ✗ (a) 「待た」is part of the negative/imperfective form in 待たない and cannot combine directly with 「つづける」.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t18-q3.why.1: ✓ (b) 「待ち」 is the V-ます stem of 「待つ」, correctly forming 「待ちつづけて」.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t18-q3.why.2: ✗ (c) 「待つ」 is the dictionary form, and there is no grammar rule allowing the dictionary form to combine directly with 「つづける」.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t18-q3.why.3: ✗ (d) 「待って」is the te-form and cannot be directly combined with「つづける」in this way, which can be confused with other structures.

default.q.pointvp_n4-t18-q4.explanation: At N4 level, the structure V-ます stem + だす expresses the beginning of an action or event, often suggesting that it starts suddenly, naturally, or emerges from within. default.q.pointvp_n4-t18-q4.why.2: ✗ (c) The pattern for continuing an action (～つづける) must use the ます-stem, with ます removed; it does not take the dictionary form (話す).
default.q.pointvp_n4-t18-q4.why.3: ✗ (d) ～つづける does not combine with a verb in the te-form (話して).

✅ Correct answer: (d) つづけていきます

default.q.pointvp_n4-t18-q6.why.1: ✗ (b) The grammar pattern ～てきます expresses an action continuing from the past to the present or going somewhere, doing something, and returning; it does not fit an ongoing situation that continues afterward.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t18-q6.why.2: ✗ (c) The Group 2 verb 続ける is incorrectly conjugated as つづきて; the correct te-form is 続けて.

The complete sentence means “As soon as she saw my face, she suddenly burst into tears.” To avoid confusion, when 急に appears, favor ～出す rather than ～続ける, which describes continuing an action. Also note that the Group 1 verb 泣く has the ます-stem なき, not ない. A typical example is: 空が暗くなって、急に雨が降り出しました (The sky grew dark, and then it suddenly started to rain).

default.q.pointvp_n4-t18-q7.why.2: ✗ (c) It is incorrect both in verb conjugation (it should be なき) and in meaning, because ～つづける expresses continuous continuation, contrary to the sudden nature of 急に.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t18-q7.why.3: ✗ (d) Incorrect semantically because V-ます + 続ける means to continue an action, so it does not fit with an adverb expressing suddenness such as 急に.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t18-q8.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (b) 飲みおわったら
The structure「V (ます-stem) + おわる」expresses completion. Combined with「飲む」, it naturally means “after finishing drinking” before throwing away the bottle.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t18-q8.explanation: The grammar pattern「verb stem ＋ おわる」expresses that an action has been completed fully and brought to an end. Combined with the conditional form「～たら」, it becomes「～おわったら」, meaning "after finishing V, ...". The complete sentence means: "After you finish drinking the soft drink, throw the plastic bottle into the trash, okay?" A similar example is:「この本を読みおわったら、図書館に返してください。」(After you finish reading this book, please return it to the library.) Remember to distinguish「～おわる」(to finish) from「～だす」(to begin), and use the context of throwing away an empty plastic bottle (ペットボトルをすてる) to choose 飲む (to drink) rather than 買う (to buy).
default.q.pointvp_n4-t18-q8.why.0: ✗ (a) 買いおわったら means “after finishing buying,” but it does not fit the practical logic: one would not throw away a plastic bottle immediately after buying a drink, before drinking it.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t18-q8.why.1: ✓ (b) 飲みおわったら combines 「飲む」 with 「～おわる」 to mean “after finishing drinking,” which is completely correct grammatically and fits the context of throwing away the empty bottle.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t18-q8.why.2: ✗ (c) 買いだしたら uses 「～だす」to mean “start buying,” which is completely wrong for this context.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t18-q8.why.3: ✗ (d) 飲みだしたら means “once one starts drinking,” which is illogical because the bottle cannot be thrown away as soon as one has just started drinking.

✅ Correct answer: (b) がんばってきた

default.q.pointvp_n4-t18-q9.explanation: The pattern「V-てくる」(verb te-form + くる), when used along a timeline, describes an action or process that has accumulated or continued from the past up to the present. The complete dialogue means: Jun: "I’m worried about whether I’ll pass tomorrow’s exam." — Teacher: "You’ve been working hard all this time, so everything will be fine." Compare: 「今まで毎日漢字を練習してきた。」(Up to now, I have practiced kanji every day.) To distinguish this point of grammar, identify the direction of time: an action accumulated from the past to the present uses「～てきた」(often with ずっと or 今まで), while an action continuing from the present into the future uses「～ていく」(with これから).
default.q.pointvp_n4-t18-q9.why.0: ✗ (a) 「がんばっていく」 indicates continuing to make an effort toward the future, so it is unsuitable for describing efforts made up to the present.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t18-q9.why.1: ✓ (b) 「がんばってきた」combined with「ずっと」accurately expresses sustained effort that began in the past and has continued up to the present.

default.q.pointvp_n4-t19-q1.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (c) すぎて
The grammar pattern ~すぎる follows the verb stem formed by removing ます from the ます-form and expresses an action exceeding a limit, leading to a negative result in the following clause.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t19-q1.explanation: The key grammar pattern is V-masu stem (remove ます) + すぎる, which becomes すぎて when connecting clauses. It describes an action performed beyond the normal or acceptable limit, often resulting in an undesirable consequence. In the question, the following clause is 「おなかをこわしました」(I got a stomachache), so 飲みすぎて is needed to show that the cause was drinking too much cold water. The complete sentence means: "I drank too much cold water, so I got a stomachache." Compare: 「昨日、甘い物を食べすぎて、歯が痛くなりました。」(Yesterday, I ate too many sweets, so my teeth started hurting.) default.q.pointvp_n4-t19-q1.why.1: ✗ (b) ~やすくて expresses that an action is easy to perform, so it does not logically connect to the following clause.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t19-q1.why.2: ✓ (c) ~すぎて expresses drinking more than the normal amount, which directly caused the stomach trouble.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t19-q1.why.3: ✗ (d) ～にくくて means that something is difficult to do, which is the complete opposite of the context.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t19-q10.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (b) 寒くありません
The negative comparison pattern 「A は B ほど + negative form」means “A is not as...as B,” so the predicate following 「アラスカほど」must be negative.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t19-q10.explanation: The negative comparison pattern 「N1 は N2 ほど + adjective/verb in the negative form (〜ない / 〜ありません)」 means that N1 is not as ... as N2. It is used when the degree of N1 does not reach the level represented by N2. Applied to the exercise, the dialogue is 「北海道は寒いですか。」-「アラスカほど寒くありませんよ。」(Smith: "Is Hokkaido cold?" - Yamamoto: "It is not as cold as Alaska."). Another example is: 「今年の夏は去年ほど暑くないです。」(This summer is not as hot as last summer.) When you see a noun followed by 「ほど」 in this comparison pattern, the following clause must be negative, allowing you to eliminate affirmative choices such as 「寒そうです」, 「寒いです」, and 「寒すぎます」.

default.q.pointvp_n4-t19-q10.why.2: ✗ (c) 「寒いです」is an affirmative form meaning “it is cold.” It is grammatically incorrect because the comparison pattern 「～ほど」must be used with a negative predicate.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t19-q10.why.3: ✗ (d) 「寒すぎます」expresses that something is “too cold,” exceeding a limit; its affirmative form does not fit this grammatical structure.

The grammar pattern 「V-ます (ます removed) ＋ にくい」expresses difficulty performing an action, here because the road is covered with gravel.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t19-q2.explanation: The pattern 「V-stem + にくい」 expresses that an action is difficult to perform or occur because of objective characteristics, circumstances, or external conditions. In this sentence, 「いしが多くて」 (there are many stones) makes walking difficult: 「この道はいしが多くて歩きにくいから、ほかの道を通ります。」 (This road has many stones and is difficult to walk on, so we will take another road.) Another example is: 「この字は小さすぎて読みにくいです。」 (These characters are too small to read easily.) Remember the contrasting suffixes 「〜やすい」 (easy to do) and 「〜にくい」 (difficult to do). When the sentence mentions an obstacle or disadvantage, 「〜にくい」 is the appropriate choice.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t19-q2.why.0: ✗ (a) 「〜たい」expresses the speaker’s desire (“want to go”), so it is entirely inappropriate in a clause giving the reason that the road is covered with gravel.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t19-q2.why.1: ✗ (b) 「〜やすい」means “easy to do” (“easy to walk”), which directly conflicts with the condition of a rough, rocky road.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t19-q2.why.2: ✗ (c) 「〜すぎる」 indicates exceeding a limit (“go too much”) and does not form a meaningful sentence in this context.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t19-q2.why.3: ✓ (d) 「〜にくい」combines with a verb stem to mean “difficult to do something,” correctly expressing that the rocky road is difficult to walk on.

The pattern V-stem + やすい describes an action that is easy to perform or an object that is easy to use, providing an appropriate reason for the speaker’s liking it.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t19-q3.explanation: The structure 「ます-form stem + やすい」turns a verb into an i-adjective meaning that an action is easy to perform or that an object is convenient and easy to use. The complete sentence means: "This computer is easy to use, so I really like it." Another example is: 「このペンはとても書きやすいです。」(This pen is very easy to write with.) Remember the contrasting grammar patterns 「～やすい」(easy to do) and 「～にくい」(difficult to do). Also distinguish them from 「～たい」, which expresses the speaker's desire and does not describe an object's characteristics.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t19-q3.why.0: ✗ (a) Incorrect because V-masu + たい expresses the desire to do something, not how easy an object is to operate.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t19-q3.why.1: ✓ (b) Correct because the structure V-masu + やすい means “easy to do”; 使いやすい (easy to use) therefore reasonably explains why the speaker likes the computer.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t19-q3.why.2: ✗ (c) This is incorrect because the V-masu + すぎる pattern means “to do something excessively,” usually with a negative nuance, which does not fit the following expression of fondness.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t19-q3.why.3: ✗ (d) The pattern V-masu + にくい means “difficult to do,” which is completely inconsistent with the following result, “I like it.”

The structure 「なかなか + verb in the ない-form」 describes something that fails to happen despite expectations, fitting the context of the bus being delayed by heavy traffic.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t19-q4.explanation: When the adverb 「なかなか」 is combined with a verb in the negative form (～ない), it means "cannot... easily" or "keeps failing to..." and describes something progressing slowly, with difficulty, or not happening as expected. In the context of heavy morning traffic causing delays, the complete sentence means: "Because the roads are crowded in the morning, the bus never seems to arrive." A similar example is: 「薬を飲みましたが、熱がなかなか下がりません。」 (Although I took medicine, my fever still will not go down.) To avoid confusion, remember that 「なかなか + affirmative」 is used for praise, meaning "quite" or "very," whereas unexpected delay or inconvenience requires the negative form 「なかなか～ない」.

default.q.pointvp_n4-t19-q4.why.1: ✗ (b) 来るis affirmative, whereas なかなか, when expressing that something has not been achieved as expected, must be used with a negative form.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t19-q4.why.2: ✓ (c) 来ない is the negative form and correctly combines with the adverb なかなか to express that the bus still has not arrived because of traffic.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t19-q4.why.3: ✗ (d) 来た is the affirmative past form (“came”), which does not fit なかなか when expressing impatience because the vehicle has not appeared.

default.q.pointvp_n4-t19-q5.why.1: ✓ (b) Correct because 「上手ではありません」is a negative form that combines properly with 「〜ほど」to create the comparison “not as good as.”

default.q.pointvp_n4-t19-q6.explanation: The grammar pattern 「〜すぎる」 (“too...”) describes a state or action that exceeds an acceptable or standard level, often causing a negative result or inconvenience. The rules are: drop 「い」 from an い-adjective, drop 「な」 from a na-adjective, and remove 「ます」 from the ます-form of a verb. In this sentence, the correct translation is: "These shoes are too tight, so I can't fit into them." A similar example is 「このスープは熱すぎて、飲めません。」(This soup is too hot to drink.) default.q.pointvp_n4-t19-q6.why.1: ✗ (b) 「小さな」is an attributive form used only to modify a following noun; it does not come before the auxiliary verb 「〜すぎる」.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t19-q6.why.2: ✗ (c) 「小さい」 has not dropped its final 「い」, violating the inflection rule for combining with 「〜すぎる」.

The adverb 「なかなか」 commonly combines with a negative potential form to express that, despite making an effort, one still cannot accomplish something.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t19-q8.explanation: In N4 grammar, the adverb「なかなか」combined with a verb in the negative form, especially the negative potential form, means "cannot seem to..." or "no matter how much one tries, it does not..." It describes something that does not proceed as expected despite considerable effort. The complete sentence means: "The kanji is so difficult that I just cannot seem to remember it." Compare:「薬を飲みましたが、熱がなかなか下がりません。」(I took medicine, but my fever just will not go down.) When you see「なかなか」after a clause describing difficulty, look for a negative ending, especially a negative potential form such as「～られません / ～できません」, rather than a desiderative or affirmative form.

✅ Correct answer: (d) すぎ
The pattern V (ます-stem) + すぎる expresses doing or being more than is normal. Here, 「つかれすぎて」 means “being too tired,” resulting in an inability to continue walking.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t19-q9.explanation: In JLPT N4, the grammar pattern 「V-ます stem + すぎる」means "to do something excessively." It describes an action or state that exceeds a reasonable limit and causes a negative result. The complete exchange can be translated as: Yamada: "You don't look well lately." — Tanaka: "I am so exhausted that I can no longer walk." A similar example is: 「昨日、お酒を飲みすぎて、頭が痛いです。」 (I drank too much alcohol yesterday, so I have a headache now.) Do not confuse it with 「～やすい」 (easy to / prone to), because 「つかれやすい」describes a general tendency or constitution, while the degree adverb 「とても」combined with the immediate result 「すぐ歩けなくなってしまう」requires 「つかれすぎる」to express overwhelming exhaustion.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t19-q9.why.0: ✗ (a) The pattern「～たがる」expresses a third person’s desire and does not combine with the stative verb「つかれる」.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t19-q9.why.1: ✗ (b) The pattern「Vます + にくい」means “difficult to do,” making the sentence mean “very difficult to get tired,” which contradicts the following clause.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t19-q9.why.2: ✗ (c) The pattern Vます + やすいexpresses a tendency for something to be easy to do, so it is unnatural with「とても」to indicate exhaustion leading to being unable to go.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t19-q9.why.3: ✓ (d) The pattern 「Vます + すぎる」indicates exceeding the normal limit. つかれすぎて (being excessively tired) fits perfectly as the reason the person cannot walk.

default.q.pointvp_n4-t2-q11.explanation: The key grammar pattern is `V-て + から` (after doing V, ...), which emphasizes the clear sequence of two actions: the first action is completed before the second begins. To form the complete sentence, place the modifying clause `父から もらった` before the noun `ケーキを`, creating “the cake received from my father,” then connect it to `食べてから` and finish with the predicate `ねました`. The complete sentence is 「きのう、父からもらったケーキを食べてからねました。」, meaning: “Yesterday, I went to bed after eating the cake my father gave me.” A similar example is: 宿題をしてから、テレビを見ました。(After doing my homework, I watched TV.) For this type of ordering question, identify the final predicate first (`ねました`), then find `V-てから` (`食べてから`) and the noun phrase with its modifier (`もらったケーキ`).

default.q.pointvp_n4-t2-q11.why.2: ✗ (c) ねました is the main predicate in the past tense and completes the sentence, so it must be in the fourth and final position.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t2-q11.why.3: ✗ (d) ケーキを is a noun phrase functioning as the object, so it must come second, before 食べてから.

The pattern 「[giver] は/が [recipient] に [thing] を あげます」describes the speaker, or someone on the speaker's side, giving something to another person. default.q.pointvp_n4-t2-q2.why.2: ✗ (c) 「くれました」is used when someone else gives or does something for me, so it cannot be used with the subject 「私は」.

default.q.pointvp_n4-t20-q1.verdict:

The grammar 「V-たばかり」 describes an action that has just occurred from the speaker’s subjective perspective. Combined with 「なのに」, 「〜たばかりなのに」 expresses surprise or regret when the result contradicts expectations.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t20-q1.explanation: Complete sentence:「このかさは先週買ったばかりなのに、もうこわれました。」(I only bought this umbrella last week, but it has already broken.) The key grammar pattern is「V-た + ばかり」, which describes an action that has just been completed according to the speaker’s subjective perception. Because it functions like a noun, it combines with「のに」as「〜たばかりなのに」to express dissatisfaction or regret about an unexpected result. Learners often confuse「〜たばかり」with「〜たところ」. The key difference is that「〜たところ」requires the actual time gap to be extremely short, such as a few minutes, and does not normally combine with a specific time expression such as「先週」or「先月」. In contrast,「〜たばかり」is based on the speaker’s perception and can be used with「先週」. Example: このパソコンは先月買ったばかりなのに、もう動かなくなりました。(I only bought this computer last month, but it has already stopped working.)

default.q.pointvp_n4-t20-q1.why.1: ✗ (b) The structure「V-たところ」is used only for something that has just happened, so it cannot be used with a time expression such as「先週」(last week).
default.q.pointvp_n4-t20-q1.why.2: ✗ (c) The conditional form 「買ったら」(if/after buying) cannot be followed directly by the contrastive conjunction 「なのに」grammatically.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t20-q1.why.3: ✓ (d) The pattern 「V-たばかり」combines correctly with 「なのに」in 「買ったばかりなのに」, expressing that something broke even though it had just been bought the previous week.

The complete sentence means: “Tappu doesn’t eat vegetables, so he eats nothing but meat.” A similar example is 「お酒を飲まないんです。それで、ウーロン茶にします。」 (“I don’t drink alcohol, so I’ll have oolong tea”). To avoid exam traps, distinguish 〜んです, which explains a fact or reason, from 〜たがる, which expresses a third person’s desire, and 〜てほしい, which expresses a request or wish for someone to do something.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t6-q8.why.0: ✓ (a) The short negative form 食べない combines with 〜んです to form a logical explanatory structure leading to the result that only meat is eaten in the following clause.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t6-q8.why.1: ✗ (b) The pattern 〜たがる expresses a third person’s desire, which conflicts with the context leading to eating only meat.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t6-q8.why.2: ✗ (c) The pattern 〜てほしい expresses the speaker’s wish for someone else to do something, so it is inappropriate both structurally and semantically in this sentence.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t6-q8.why.3: ✗ (d) The pattern 〜てほしくない expresses a desire for someone not to do something, so it does not fit a statement describing the subject's actual eating.

✅ Correct answer: (a) いたい
When expressing the speaker's own physical sensation or condition in the first person, the i-adjective「いたい」is used directly with「〜んですが」to give a reason before making a request.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t6-q9.explanation: In Japanese, when expressing one’s own emotions or physical sensations in the first person, use the i-adjective directly in the plain form with 「〜んですが」 (i-adjective + んですが). This creates a polite introductory tone before making a request or asking permission with 「〜てもいいですか」. The complete dialogue means: “Jun: ‘Excuse me, teacher. I have a stomachache. May I leave early?’ — Teacher: ‘Are you all right? Go home and get plenty of rest.’” A similar example is: 「あたまがいたいんですが、少し横になってもいいですか。」 (I have a headache. May I lie down for a while?) The suffix 「〜がる / 〜がっている」, as in choices b and d, is used when observing and inferring another person’s feelings from their behavior or expressions. It is not used to state one’s own feelings directly.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t6-q9.why.0: ✓ (a) Correctly expresses the speaker's own feeling of pain (first person) using the original -i adjective いたい.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t6-q9.why.1: ✗ (b) いたがっている is used to describe a third person’s expression of or feeling of pain; it is not used for oneself.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t6-q9.why.2: ✗ (c) This is grammatically incorrect and completely inappropriate for a situation in which the speaker has a stomachache and needs to ask to go home.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t6-q9.why.3: ✗ (d) The pattern いたがる expresses a third person’s apparent desire or feelings, so it is not used for the first person.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t7-q1.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (c) しまいました
The grammar V-て + しまいました expresses an unfortunate event that happened unintentionally, often with a feeling of regret.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t7-q1.explanation: The grammar pattern V-て + しまう, in its polite past form ～てしまいました, follows a verb’s て-form to indicate that something happened accidentally or against expectation, often expressing the speaker’s disappointment or regret. The complete sentence means: “I dropped the glass and accidentally broke it.” Compare: 「宿題を家に忘れてしまいました。」(I accidentally left my homework at home.) To avoid choice (d), remember that「~終わる」means finishing an action and must follow the ます-stem, as in 読み終わる; it never follows the て-form.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t7-q1.why.0: ✗ (a) Japanese has no grammatical structure combining the te-form of a verb with「しました」.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t7-q1.why.1: ✗ (b) The pattern 「~ておく (ときました)」indicates advance preparation or maintaining a state, so it is unsuitable for an unexpected incident.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t7-q1.why.2: ✓ (c) The pattern 「~てしまう (しまいました)」expresses an action that accidentally occurred and caused an unfortunate consequence beyond the speaker's control.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t7-q1.why.3: ✗ (d) The verb 「終わりました」 expresses the completion of an action and follows a V-ます stem, not a te-form.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t7-q10.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (d) おいて
This sentence uses the grammar pattern「V-て + おく」, meaning to leave something in a certain state. With the verb 置く (to put or leave), it forms the polite request「置いておいてください」.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t7-q10.explanation: The structure 「V-て + おく」, including the request form 「V-ておいてください」, follows a verb in the te-form and expresses doing something in advance or leaving a state unchanged. In the question, the adverb 「そのまま」(just as it is) shows that the speaker wants the book to remain where it is. Therefore, the main verb 「置く」(to put or leave) combines with the auxiliary verb to form the characteristic expression 「置いておいてください」. The complete dialogue means: Yamamoto asks, “What should I do with this book?” and Tanaka replies, “Please just leave it there.” Another example is: 「まだ使っているので、ハサミを出しておいてください。」(I am still using them, so please leave the scissors out.) To avoid confusing it with 「~てある」, remember that 「~てある」describes a static resultant state and is not used with the request form 「~てください」, whereas 「~ておいてください」asks someone to carry out or maintain an action or state.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t7-q10.why.0: ✗ (a) Japanese grammar has no structure 「V-て + して + ください」 for expressing leaving something in its current state.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t7-q10.why.1: ✗ (b) The pattern 「V-て + ある」indicates an existing resultant state and is not used in the requesting form 「~てあってください」.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t7-q10.why.2: ✗ (c) The pattern 「V-て + くる」 expresses movement toward the speaker or a change over time. It does not fit the context of keeping an object in place.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t7-q10.why.3: ✓ (d) The verb 置く (to put or leave) combines with 「V-て + おく」. In the request form, 「置いておいてください」 means “Please leave it there.”
default.q.pointvp_n4-t7-q11.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (c) しまって
The complete sentence is formed in the order b - a - c - d (ご飯を → 食べて → しまって → ください), so the third word in the position marked with an asterisk (*) is (c) しまって.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t7-q11.explanation: The N4 pattern「V-て + しまう」can express not only regret but also the complete, decisive finishing of an action. In a polite request, it becomes「V-て + しまって + ください」, meaning “please finish doing...” or “please consume it all.” The complete sentence is:「もう出かける時間だから、早くご飯を食べてしまってください。」(It is almost time to go out, so please hurry up and finish your meal.) Example:「この本を今日中に読んでしまってください。」(Please finish reading this book today.) Build it by combining the object「ご飯を」with「食べて」, then adding「しまって」and ending with「ください」.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t7-q11.why.0: ✗ (a) It should come in the second position after the object ご飯を to connect with the auxiliary verb しまって.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t7-q11.why.1: ✗ (b) It is in the first position as the object of the action 食べて.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t7-q11.why.2: ✓ (c) It occupies the third starred position and is conjugated in the te-form to combine with ください, forming a request to complete the action.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t7-q11.why.3: ✗ (d) It belongs in the fourth and final position to complete the polite request structure ~てください.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t7-q12.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (c) ちゃんと
The complete order is ちゃんと (c) → 勉強して (b) → おいて (d) → ください (a), so the first starred position is (c) ちゃんと.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t7-q12.explanation: The completed sentence is 「来週試験があるから、ちゃんと勉強しておいてください。」, meaning: “There’s an exam next week, so please study carefully in advance.” The key grammar point is 「V-て + おいてください」, combining the preparation pattern V-ておく with the request or advice form ください. It is used when advising someone to complete an action beforehand in preparation for an upcoming event. Here, the adverb 「ちゃんと」 (properly, diligently) directly modifies the study action 「勉強して」. For this type of question, first assemble the fixed grammar sequence 「勉強して + おいて + ください」 (order b-d-a), then place the adverb (c) first, at the position marked by the star. Another example is: 「会議の前に、資料を読んでおいてください。」 (Please read the materials in advance before the meeting.)
default.q.pointvp_n4-t7-q12.why.0: ✗ (a) ください is the polite imperative ending used to make a request or give advice, so it must appear at the end of the sentence (position 4).
default.q.pointvp_n4-t7-q12.why.1: ✗ (b) 勉強して is the te-form of the verb and comes after the adverb to connect to the auxiliary verb おいて in the following position (position 2).
default.q.pointvp_n4-t7-q12.why.2: ✓ (c) ちゃんとis an adverb meaning “properly” or “carefully,” and it occupies position 1 (the star) to modify the entire following phrase describing studying.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t7-q12.why.3: ✗ (d) おいて is the te-form of the auxiliary verb おく in the structure 〜ておく (“to prepare in advance”), and occupies the third position before ください.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t7-q2.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (b) おいて
Adding「おいて」to「行って」forms the preparation pattern「〜ておいてください」, which fits the context of using the restroom before a 3-hour bus ride.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t7-q2.explanation: The grammar pattern「V-て + おく」, in the polite request form「V-ておいてください」, describes doing something in advance as preparation for a future event. The complete sentence means: "Since we will be riding the bus for about three hours, please use the restroom beforehand." Distinguish it from「〜てある」: 「〜ておく」emphasizes the subject's preparatory action, while「〜てある」emphasizes the resulting state of something after an action has been performed. Contrastive example: 「会議の前に、資料をコピーしておいてください。」(Please make copies of the materials before the meeting.)
default.q.pointvp_n4-t7-q2.why.0: ✗ (a) して: The phrase 「行ってしてください」does not form a valid grammar pattern and is structurally incorrect.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t7-q2.why.1: ✓ (b) おいて: Combined with a verb’s te-form, 「〜ておいてください」means “please do something in advance as preparation.”
default.q.pointvp_n4-t7-q2.why.2: ✗ (c) あって: The pattern 「〜てある」 expresses the resulting state of a transitive verb, so it cannot be used with the intransitive verb 「行く」 to give advice about preparing in advance.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t7-q2.why.3: ✗ (d) おきて is the te-form of「起きる」(to wake up); inserting it into the sentence would create an illogical and grammatically incorrect meaning.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t7-q3.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (d) います
The adverbial phrase 「さっきから」, meaning “since a little while ago,” combines with 「V-ています」 to describe an action that began in the past and is still continuing.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t7-q3.explanation: The pattern「V-て + います」combined with time expressions such as「さっきから」(since a little while ago) or「朝から」(since this morning) indicates an action that began earlier and is still continuing. The complete sentence means: "My younger brother has been studying in his room since a little while ago." Another example is「母はさっきから台所で料理を作っています。」(My mother has been cooking in the kitchen since a little while ago). When a starting-point expression「～から」appears with a human action verb, prioritize the progressive form「～ています」over patterns expressing preparation「～ておく」, a state resulting from someone else's action「～てある」, or an accidental completion「～てしまう」.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t7-q3.why.0: ✗ (a) 「～てしまいました」expresses a completely finished action or regret, so it does not fit the continuing meaning of「さっきから」.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t7-q3.why.1: ✗ (b) 「～ておきます」indicates doing something in advance for the future; it does not express an action in progress.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t7-q3.why.2: ✗ (c) 「～てあります」expresses the resultant state of something after an intentional action; it is not used when the subject is a person performing an action.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t7-q3.why.3: ✓ (d) 「～ています」combines with「勉強する」to indicate the continuing state of studying, maintained from earlier until now.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t7-q4.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (a) 走っています
The pattern verb te-form + います, combined with the frequency adverb 毎日, expresses a regular habit or repeated action.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t7-q4.explanation: In addition to indicating an ongoing action, V-て + います is commonly used at N4 level to describe habits or regular routines over an extended period, especially with frequency expressions such as 毎日 (every day) and よく (often). The complete sentence means: “My grandfather is 90 years old this year, but he is still very fit and goes jogging in the park every day.” A similar example is 「私は毎朝６時に起きて、本を読んでいます。」(I get up at 6 every morning and read a book.) To avoid a common trap, remember that 走る (to run) is a special Group 1 verb, so its て-form is 走って, not 走りて. Also, ～てある applies only to transitive verbs, so it cannot be used with the intransitive verb 走る.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t7-q4.why.0: ✓ (a) The verb 走る changes to the te-form 走って and combines with います to express a repeated daily habit.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t7-q4.why.1: ✗ (b) 走ってしまいます expresses an accidental action, regret, or an action completed fully; it is not used for an everyday habit.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t7-q4.why.2: ✗ (c) 走りています is grammatically incorrect because 走る is a Group 1 verb, whose te-form is 走って.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t7-q4.why.3: ✗ (d) 走ってあります is grammatically incorrect because the ～てある pattern is used only with transitive verbs to express a resulting state, whereas 走る is an intransitive verb.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t7-q5.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (c) 買って
The pattern「Vてあります」describes something that has been done and prepared for a specific purpose.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t7-q5.explanation: The grammar pattern 「transitive verb in the て-form + あります」 expresses a state resulting from a deliberate action performed as preparation. Therefore, 「買う」(to buy) must change to its て-form 「買って」. The complete sentence translates as: "The wine and soft drinks for the party have already been bought." Another similar example is: 「誕生日のケーキはもう予約してあります。」(The birthday cake has already been ordered.) Distinguish 「Vてあります」, which emphasizes a prepared resulting state and always uses a transitive verb, from 「Vています」, which commonly describes a state with an intransitive verb or an ongoing action with a transitive verb.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t7-q5.why.0: ✗ (a) 買い is the verb stem formed by removing ます and does not combine directly with あります in a structure expressing a resultant state.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t7-q5.why.1: ✗ (b) 買った is the ta-form (past), so it violates the verb conjugation rule for use before あります.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t7-q5.why.2: ✓ (c) 買って is the te-form of the transitive verb 買う and correctly combines with あります in 「Vてあります」to indicate that something has already been purchased and left prepared.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t7-q5.why.3: ✗ (d) 買う is the dictionary form, so it is grammatically incorrect before the auxiliary verb あります.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t7-q6.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (d) いる
The verb こわれる (壊れる) is an intransitive verb describing a change of state. Combined with 「~ている」, it expresses the object’s current broken state.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t7-q6.explanation: In N4 grammar, the pattern「intransitive verb in the te-form + いる」is commonly used to describe the resulting state of an action or objective change that has occurred and still remains. The complete sentence means: "Because the television is broken, I cannot watch it." To understand this usage, compare: 「窓が閉まっていますから、部屋が暑いです。」(Because the window is closed, the room is hot.) To distinguish it from option (a), remember that「intransitive verb + ている」describes an objective state, while「transitive verb + てある」emphasizes a state resulting from a deliberate human action.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t7-q6.why.0: ✗ (a) The structure 「~てある」 combines only with transitive verbs to express a deliberately created state. It cannot be used with the intransitive verb こわれる.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t7-q6.why.1: ✗ (b) The structure 「~ておく」(past form: ておいた) expresses an action performed in advance for a particular purpose, so it is unsuitable both semantically and grammatically in this sentence.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t7-q6.why.2: ✗ (c) The structure 「~てもらう」(past form: てもらった) expresses receiving help from someone else, so it is completely incompatible with an inanimate subject.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t7-q6.why.3: ✓ (d) The pattern 「intransitive verb in the te-form + いる」is the correct structure for describing the resulting state of an event that has occurred and whose effects continue in the present.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t7-q7.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (c) 読んでいません
「まだ」 (“still” or “not yet”) with the 「～ていません」 form describes an expected action that has not yet been carried out at the time of speaking.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t7-q7.explanation: The N4 pattern 「まだ＋V-ていません」 uses the adverb まだ with a verb in the negative te-form to indicate that an intended or planned action has still not been completed at the present time. The complete sentence means: “I still have not read the book I borrowed last week.” For example: 「レポートはもう出しましたか。— いいえ、まだ出していません。」 (“Have you submitted the report yet? — No, I haven’t submitted it yet.”). To express that an action has not yet been performed, Japanese uses 「まだ～ていません」, not the past negative 「～ませんでした」 or the result pattern 「～てあります」.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t7-q7.why.0: ✗ (a) The structure「V-ておきます」describes an action done in advance as preparation, so the negative form does not fit with the adverb まだ.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t7-q7.why.1: ✗ (b) The structure 「V-てしまいます」expresses accidentally doing something or completing it entirely, carrying an affirmative meaning, so it cannot be used with まだ.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t7-q7.why.2: ✓ (c) 「まだ＋V-ていません」is the correct grammar pattern for indicating that a planned action has not yet been carried out.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t7-q7.why.3: ✗ (d) The structure 「V-てあります」describes a state resulting from an intentionally completed action; it is not used for something that has not yet happened.

default.q.pointvp_n4-t7-q8.why.1: ✗ (b) The pattern 「～てほしい」expresses the desire for someone else to do something for the speaker, which conflicts with the context of doing it 「一人で」.

The complete dialogue means: Yamada: "What a beautiful plate. I really want to buy it, but I wonder whether it is expensive." – Tanaka: "The price has already been written there." The key difference between 〜ておく and 〜てある is that 〜ておく focuses on an action performed in advance as preparation, often with the particle を, whereas 〜てある focuses on the resulting state visible now and is used with the particle が.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t7-q9.why.0: ✗ (a) 書いてしまう: The 〜てしまう form expresses an accidentally completed action that causes regret, or an action completed entirely; it is not used to indicate an existing state.

default.q.pointvp_n4-t7-q9.why.3: ✗ (d) 書いてほしい: The pattern 〜てほしい expresses a desire for someone else to do something for the speaker, so it is completely inappropriate in this context.

✅ Correct answer: (b) 来てくれました
The subject, a friend (ともだちが), came to help the speaker, providing a benefit to the speaker. This fits the pattern Vてくれました.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t8-q1.explanation: The pattern `[another person] が [me/someone in my group] に + Vてくれる` (past: `Vてくれました`) describes another person voluntarily doing something helpful for the speaker, with a feeling of gratitude. default.q.pointvp_n4-t9-q7.explanation: The structure「V1-る + とか、V2-る + とか」lists representative actions or options ("doing things like ... and ..." or "either ... or ..."). It generally uses the plain form and is common in casual conversation. With the future time expression「今度の夏休み」(the coming summer vacation), both listed actions use the dictionary form to express possible plans. The complete sentence means: "My son says that he will either work part-time or travel during the coming summer vacation." For example:「週末は部屋を掃除するとか映画を見るとかして過ごします」(On weekends, I spend my time doing things like cleaning my room or watching movies.) Pay attention to the time expression when choosing the tense, and remember that the particle「とか」never follows the te-form, so choice (d) can be eliminated.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t9-q7.why.0: ✗ (a) Combining the volitional form (しよう) with the negative form (行かない) does not create a logical parallel structure and does not fit a future intention.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t9-q7.why.1: ✓ (b) Correct because both verbs are in the dictionary form (辞書形: するとか / 行くとか), creating a correct parallel listing structure for upcoming plans.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t9-q7.why.2: ✗ (c) The verb 行った is in the past tense (た形), which conflicts with the future time reference 今度の夏休み (“the upcoming summer vacation”).
default.q.pointvp_n4-t9-q7.why.3: ✗ (d) The listing particle とか does not combine directly with a verb in the て-form (行ってとか).
default.q.pointvp_n4-t9-q8.verdict:
✅ Correct answer: (a) やめる
The pattern 「V (plain form) + という話」quotes the content of an event, story, or piece of news that was heard.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t9-q8.explanation: The grammar pattern 「V (plain form / 普通形) + という + noun」, as in 話, 噂, or ニュース, is an important N4 structure used to specify or quote the content of the abstract noun that follows. In this sentence, the content of the story (話) is the objective fact that "Mr./Ms. Nishida will quit the company," so the verb must be in the dictionary form 「やめる」. The complete sentence means: "I heard that Mr./Ms. Nishida will quit the company." Compare it with: 「来月、新しい先生が来るという話を聞きました。」 (I heard that a new teacher will come next month.) For objective events or news introduced by 「〜という話」, choose a plain-form verb describing the action rather than forms expressing personal intention or desire, such as 〜たい, 〜よう, or 〜てほしい.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t9-q8.why.0: ✓ (a) The dictionary-form verb やめる comes before 「という話」as a modifier, expressing the news that Mr./Ms. Nishida will quit the job.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t9-q8.why.1: ✗ (b) The ending やめたい expresses the speaker's own desire, so it is not suitable for conveying objective information about another person's action.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t9-q8.why.2: ✗ (c) The volitional ending やめよう is used to make a suggestion or express the speaker's own decision, so it cannot be used to modify a noun and form this news-related clause.
default.q.pointvp_n4-t9-q8.why.3: ✗ (d) The ending やめないでほしい expresses a request or wish for someone not to do something, so it does not fit a context in which an event is being reported.
